text: You've now seen all three pieces separately: Git as source of truth, pull instead of push, and continuous reconciliation against drift. This lesson puts them side by side against a plain CI/CD pipeline, so you can point at exactly what's different, stage by stage.

Nothing about building and testing changes. Both pipelines check out code, run tests, build an image, and push it to a registry. The split happens at the last stage. In plain CI/CD, that stage runs kubectl apply straight against the cluster. In GitOps, the pipeline's last act is a commit instead — it bumps the image tag in the manifest repo and opens a pull request. CI never touches the cluster at all.

Build and test stay exactly where they were. What moves is everything after that: cluster credentials shift from the pipeline into the in-cluster agent alone, the trigger for a deploy becomes a commit landing on a watched branch instead of a pipeline run finishing, and drift detection and a full audit trail appear for the first time, courtesy of the agent's reconciliation loop and Git's own history.

Promotion changes shape too. In plain CI/CD, promoting to production usually means re-running the same pipeline against a different kubectl context. In GitOps, the staging overlay already has the new image tag, and promoting means opening a pull request that copies that change into the production overlay — so whoever reviews it is looking at the literal diff of what's about to run in production.

None of this is free — merging to the watched branch is the deploy, so branch protection and PR review on the manifest repo matter as much as the approval gate they replace. And a team that keeps YAML in Git but still lets CI run kubectl apply directly hasn't adopted GitOps at all; it's kept the push model and just moved the files. Real GitOps needs all four principles from this chapter together: declarative, versioned, pulled automatically, and continuously reconciled.
